title: Non-differentiable realistic fluid renderer: particles to a believable liquid
objective: Build a high-quality, NON-differentiable renderer that turns the 2D MLS-MPM weakly-compressible fluid's particle cloud into side-on frames that read as a real liquid, like water in a glass tank. The physics is reused from the fluid path of sim/material_showcase.py (weakly compressible pressure from the tracked volume ratio J); the deliverable is the renderer, not the simulation. Two dynamic scenes are shown -- a fluid ball dropped into a shallow pool (splash crown and droplets) and a dam-break column collapse (rolling wave into the far wall) -- each as an mp4 and a hero still, plus a 'how it's built' breakdown figure. Visual quality is the only graded axis: this makes no claim about physical accuracy, real-time performance, or differentiability, and is not meant to be any of those.
findings: The renderer is a screen-space fluid pipeline (all numpy/scipy, headless to mp4) and it clearly reads as liquid rather than a particle scatter. Per frame it (1) splats the particles into a high-resolution density field with a Gaussian kernel (metaballs) and takes an anti-aliased density isocontour as the liquid surface, with a screen-space surface normal lifted from the 2D density gradient (flat interior faces the viewer, the rim grazes); (2) shades the body with Beer-Lambert depth/absorption color so thin water is pale translucent cyan and thick water is deep saturated blue, refracts a structured studio background offset by the surface normal so the background visibly bends through the liquid, blends an environment reflection against that refracted body by a Schlick-Fresnel term that brightens the grazing rims and wave edges, and adds a tight Blinn-Phong specular glint plus a broad wet sheen; (3) paints whitewater foam where the surface moves fast (crests, splash crowns) or the fluid is thin and broken (spray, sheet edges, droplets), gated to a surface band so particle discreteness does not speckle the calm interior; (4) finishes with bloom on the highlights, a subtle floor reflection, a vignette, and a filmic tone map. Both scenes run stable (n_grid=128, 21k particles for the ball drop, 24k for the dam break, no non-finite values). The ball drop resolves into a crown cavity with curling arms and whitewater tips; the dam break produces a whitewater wave front with droplets running ahead, a run-up jet climbing the far wall with a ballistic droplet arc, and a returning wave that curls over an enclosed pocket of air -- a recognizable breaking-wave tube. Output is 1000x1000 at 150 frames, 30 fps. The render-look-improve loop was run explicitly and every intermediate was viewed: an initial pass that coated the whole body in blotchy foam, a second that washed the water milky-pale, and a background whose light bars read as columns were each caught by looking at the frame and fixed (surface-gated coherent foam, a darker deep-water body with the uniform sheen cut, and soft localized softbox glows).
hypothesis: The image reads as water because a small stack of cheap, well-chosen cues each supplies a specific recognition signal, and they compound. The largest single jump from dots to liquid is the reconstructed surface: a smooth metaball isocontour replaces a cloud of points with a continuous boundary, which is the precondition for every optical cue that follows. Of those cues, refraction of a structured background is the strongest realism lever, because a bent background is something no scatter plot can imitate; it only works when the background actually carries structure to displace, which is why the scene is lit with soft studio sources and a horizon rather than a flat wall. Beer-Lambert depth color gives the body volume instead of a flat cutout, angle-dependent Fresnel reflection and the specular glint supply the wet sheen, and foam sells fast, torn-up motion. A structural consequence of the 2D side view is worth noting: the interior surface normal faces the viewer nearly uniformly, so a broad specular 'sheen' term washes the whole body pale if left large, while the tight high-exponent glint correctly stays near zero on the flat interior and only flares where the normal swings at a crest or ripple. Localizing highlights to curved features rather than painting a spherical glint is therefore the physically appropriate behavior for a flat slab of water in a tank, not a shortcoming. What would test how far this generalizes: more scene types and camera framings, animated caustics on the floor, a measured absorption spectrum and index of refraction, and a genuine screen-space thickness accumulated along the view ray rather than a 2D density proxy.
limitations: This is a stylized 2D side-view render, NOT a physical light-transport simulation, and it is graded only on how convincing the image looks. The thickness that drives both the absorption and the refraction is a proxy read off a 2D density field, not a real optical path length through a 3D volume. There is no true refraction with a measured index of refraction, no caustics cast onto the floor, no inter-reflection between parts of the surface, and no measured absorption spectrum for water; the body colors and all coefficients (absorption, refraction scale, specular exponent, foam thresholds; the Fresnel F0=0.02 is the one physically grounded constant) are chosen by eye for looks. The surface normal is reconstructed by lifting a 2D gradient into a fabricated third component, so the sense of roundness is an artistic choice rather than recovered geometry. The result reaches a convincing double-take but stops short of photoreal, and the remaining gap is exactly the 3D light transport it never attempts -- an honest 'best achievable with this pipeline', not 'indistinguishable from real'. Only two scenes at one grid resolution (n_grid=128, f32) are shown; the underlying MPM fluid uses hand-tuned parameters chosen for a stable, good-looking splash (E=170, dt about 1.1-1.2e-4, low floor friction, sticky side walls), and different settings would give different splash shapes. GPU atomic-add accumulation is not bitwise reproducible, so exact splash geometry varies slightly run-to-run. No gradients, optimization, or loss are involved anywhere; the renderer is deliberately non-differentiable and offline (hard thresholds, per-pixel branches, image sampling), which is the whole point of the exercise and the opposite regime from the rest of the project.

results.caption: Dam-break collapse: a tall column of fluid released sideways runs across the floor as a whitewater wave front, jets up the far wall throwing a ballistic droplet arc, then returns as a breaking wave that curls over and traps a pocket of air. The body carries a depth gradient from pale shallow cyan to deep blue, the surface refracts the studio background and catches bright Fresnel edges, and aerated foam marks the fast crests and spray.

Hero still from the dam break at the moment the returning wave curls over an enclosed air tube, the classic breaking-wave barrel. Depth color, a bent refracted background, bright specular edges on the curling sheet, and whitewater on the crest all appear in one frame.

Fluid ball drop: a blob of liquid falls into a shallow pool, punches a cavity, and throws up a splash crown whose curling arms break into whitewater tips and droplets before the pool sloshes back level. The falling blob is a translucent tinted body with a bright waterline rim; the pool surface catches the studio light as a reflective sheen.

Hero still from the ball drop at peak splash: the impact cavity is open and the crown arms curl inward with whitewater at their tips, over a deep-blue pool that shades lighter where it thins toward the surface.

How one frame is built, left to right: the raw MPM particles as a scatter (dots, not liquid); the density field they splat into (metaballs, bright where particles cluster); the surface reconstructed from that field, shown as a clay model lit only by its reconstructed normals so the recovered shape is visible with no color; and the final shaded frame with depth color, refraction, reflection, and foam composited on.
